domains.title: Halmoni, the Grandmother Spirit
domains.subtitle: venerated grandmother of earth, ancestry, and the household
domains.lead: Halmoni is the grandmother spirit, a title of veneration given to ancestral female deities who watch over earth, lineage, and the household in Korean tradition. The name means "Grandmother" and belongs to the domain "Grandmother Spirit, Earth." Halmoni means "grandmother" in Korean, but in religious usage it becomes an honorific title for powerful female spirits who protect lineage, land, and the domestic sphere. The most famous Halmoni figure is Seolmundae Halmang of Jeju Island, a giant grandmother whose body became the landscape and whose grief created the island's geography.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Halmoni is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: Seolmundae Halmang Shapes Jeju
myths.text: The giant grandmother Seolmundae Halmang is said to have created the geography of Jeju Island with her body. When she died, her corpse became mountains, fields, and villages; her tears formed streams and coastal features.

myths.title: The Grandmother of the House
myths.text: In mainland households, Halmoni can refer to the spirit of an honoured female ancestor or to the grandmotherly form of a domestic deity. Offerings of food and wine at ancestral rites keep her favour and protection active.

myths.title: Samshin Halmoni
myths.text: The title Halmoni is added to Samshin, the three birth spirits, producing Samshin Halmoni, a single grandmotherly goddess who protects mothers and infants. This convergence shows how the title gathers female divine power across cults.

etymology.derivation: The native Korean word halmoni means "grandmother." When applied to spirits, it becomes an honorific title that elevates female ancestors and domestic goddesses to sacred status.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Halmoni, the Hangul form is 할머니. Hangul ‘할머니’ (grandmother); the term is used as a divine title for several figures, including Samshin Halmoni and the Jeju creator grandmother Seolmundae Halmang. The ASCII form halmoni is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Halmoni is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Halmoni is less a single deity than a title that gathers female sacred power across Korean religion. It overlaps with Samshin Halmoni in birth cults, with Seolmundae Halmang in Jeju landscape myth, and with household ancestor spirits in Confucian-influenced ancestral rites. Buddhist and Daoist iconography sometimes supplies visual forms for grandmother spirits, but the core identity remains indigenous. The figure challenges scholarly models that separate gods from ancestors, because Halmoni moves fluidly between both categories.
lore.culturalLegacy: Halmoni remains vivid in Korean family life through ancestral rites, folk painting, Jeju mythology, and popular media. The story of Seolmundae Halmang is retold in Jeju tourism, children's books, and regional festivals. The title also carries emotional weight in Korean diaspora communities, where grandmother figures often symbolise cultural continuity. Feminist scholars have turned to Halmoni as evidence of persistent female sacred authority in Korean religion, while environmentalists cite Seolmundae as a mythic model of embodied relationship with land.
lore.extendedMeditation: Halmoni invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
